lead: The area between two curves is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve over the interval between their intersection points. Picture thin vertical strips: each strip has height top minus bottom and width dx, so the strips sum to a definite integral. Engineers use it to measure clearance between profiles, the gap between revenue and cost curves, and visible area between plotted boundaries. Some syllabi call this area of a region between curves. Only a few universities teach this as a separate advanced topic. Vertical slices, horizontal slices, intersections, splitting, and symmetry follow.
prereq: You need: definite integrals and antiderivatives from Chapter 2.1 and Chapter 2.2.

blocks.text: Slice the region into thin vertical strips of width dx. At a fixed x, y<sub>T</sub>(x) is the top curve height and y<sub>B</sub>(x) is the bottom curve height. One strip has height y<sub>T</sub>(x) − y<sub>B</sub>(x) and area dA = [y<sub>T</sub>(x) − y<sub>B</sub>(x)] dx.

blocks.where: a and b are left and right x-limits; y<sub>T</sub> is top and y<sub>B</sub> is bottom; the integrand must be ≥0.

blocks.text: The limits a and b may be intersection points or given directly. If the curves cross, the top curve can become the bottom curve. Then the integral gives a signed net, not an area.
For y=x and y=x² on 0≤x≤1, top is y=x, bottom is y=x². Area = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup>(x−x²)dx = [x²/2 − x³/3]<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> = 1/6 square unit. The figure shows this.

Some regions are easier as thin horizontal strips of height dy. Solve each curve for x. Let x<sub>R</sub>(y) be the right curve and x<sub>L</sub>(y) the left curve. A strip has width x<sub>R</sub>(y) − x<sub>L</sub>(y) and area [x<sub>R</sub>(y) − x<sub>L</sub>(y)] dy.

blocks.where: c and d are bottom and top y-limits; x<sub>R</sub> is right and x<sub>L</sub> is left.

blocks.text: Use horizontal slices when the curves come as x=g(y), or when a vertical slice would need two top formulas. Check that right minus left is nonnegative on c≤y≤d. A positive width keeps the integral nonnegative.
For x=y² and x=4, y runs −2 to 2. Area = ∫<sub>−2</sub><sup>2</sup>(4−y²)dy = 32/3 square units. This is the same idea turned sideways; use it when vertical slices would split.

items: Set f(x)=g(x) and solve. These roots are possible limits or split points.
Sort the roots. Test one x in each interval to find which curve is on top.
Integrate top minus bottom on each interval and add the pieces.

blocks.where: |...| is absolute value; split at every crossing.

blocks.text: Symmetry can halve the work. For mirror symmetry about the y-axis, area = 2∫<sub>0</sub><sup>a</sup>[top−bottom]dx for the right half from 0 to a. For symmetry about the x-axis, use horizontal slices and double the upper half. Symmetry must match both curves and limits.

When a question says 'bounded by', solve for intersections. If limits are given, still check for crossings inside them. A crossing splits the region into separate pieces; each piece has its own top and bottom.

figure.caption: The curves y=x and y=x² meet at x=0 and x=1. The area between them is the integral of x−x², equal to 1/6.

spec.aria: The curves y=x and y=x² meet at x=0 and x=1; the area between them is 1/6.

examples.question: Find the area of the region bounded by y = x and y = x².
steps: Solve x = x²: x(1−x)=0, so x=0 and x=1. The intersection points are (0,0) and (1,1).
Test x=1/2. y=x=0.5 and y=x²=0.25, so y=x is top and y=x² is bottom on 0<x<1.
The area is positive, so the order is correct.
examples.answer: The area is 1/6 square unit, with intersection x-values 0 and 1.
examples.check:
a=0.0
b=1.0
area=(b**2/2 - b**3/3) - (a**2/2 - a**3/3)
print(area)
print(a)
print(b)

traps: Integrating top minus bottom without checking which curve is on top; after an intersection the order may swap.
Using x-limits as y-limits for horizontal slices.
Forgetting to split at a crossing; the integral then gives a signed net, not area.
Using given endpoints without checking whether curves cross inside.
Mixing dx and dy: vertical slices need y as a function of x; horizontal slices need x as a function of y.

quiz.a: A = ∫<sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup> [y<sub>T</sub>(x) − y<sub>B</sub>(x)] dx, with y<sub>T</sub> top and y<sub>B</sub> bottom.
Because top minus bottom changes sign; one integral over the whole interval would subtract one part.

quiz.q: Find area between y=√x and y=x from x=0 to 1.
Curves y=x³ and y=x meet at x=−1,0,1. Set up the total area.
quiz.a: Split: ∫<sub>−1</sub><sup>0</sup>(x³−x)dx + ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup>(x−x³)dx. On (−1,0), x³ is above x; on (0,1), x is above x³.
A = ∫<sub>c</sub><sup>d</sup> [x<sub>R</sub>(y) − x<sub>L</sub>(y)] dy, with x<sub>R</sub> right and x<sub>L</sub> left.

quiz.q: Find area bounded by x=y² and x=4.
quiz.a: Right x=4, left x=y²; y from −2 to 2. Area = ∫<sub>−2</sub><sup>2</sup>(4−y²)dy = [4y−y³/3]<sub>−2</sub><sup>2</sup> = 32/3 square units.

beyond: Not for the exam. Area between curves becomes area of a region in Unit 5, where double integrals handle more general boundaries. In practice it appears in CAD clearance checks, GIS polygon area, and gaps between probability density curves. Search next for 'area between curves', 'horizontal slices', and 'Green's theorem area'.
